messages.subject: Capter1's qustion in online lecutre.
parts:
Hi all,

I am studying distance sampling as one of the analysis methods for environmental impact assessment of seabirds. I'm new to R language and statistics, so I don't know if it's okay to ask here. When I create a model in the nest example in an online lecture (key function = half normal, without term), the AIC value is automatically calculated. At this time, is the number of bins used for model fitting automatically determined?
I'm checking the function myself with python because I want to understand distance sampling accurately. The algorithm sequence divides the observed data into regular intervals and then extracts the histogram. Select an appropriate key function and curve fit the histogram and model. After fitting model, make pdf and calculating the AIC, but the result is different from R. Python = 928.112(with 12bins), R = 928.134(it fixed.. why?). Am I misunderstanding?

Thanks,

messages.author: 75e0b0abcbafbc7d
messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Capter1's qustion in online lecutre.
parts:
I suspect you are referring to the duck nest data set used in the first chapter of the online workshop materials. That data set used exact distances (rather than binned distances). The maximum likelihood work to produce the parameter estimates of the half normal detection function operates on the exact distances.

The creation of the plots showing the histogram of detection distances with the detection function superimposed is not part of the fitting process, merely for visual depiction. There are two arguments to the plot()​ function, nc​ where you can specify the number of bins you want or breaks​ where you specify a vector of breakpoints to use in the visual depiction of the histogram. I hope that is useful.

messages.subject: Re: {Suspected Spam} [distance-sampling] Capter1's qustion in online lecutre.
parts:
Correction to my previous response.

The duck nest data used in Chapter 1 of the online workshop (using Distance for Windows software) is binned into 8 distance categories, each 1 foot in width.

The number of bins used for model fitting is determined by the input data. Eight bins existed in the data, the software cannot change that. I'm not sure how your Python code was able to compute an AIC score using 12 bins.

The AIC score computed by Distance for Windows from the half normal key function without adjustments for the binned duck nest data is 2220.84.


Duck nest data is also provided in Chapter 7 of the online workshop materials to demonstrate analysis using the R package Distance. Results of the R analysis in chapter 7 for a half normal without adjustments produces the AIC score of 928.134 as you report. Here I reiterate my explanation from previous message: data are not binned to compute the likelihood, exact values are used. I cannot speak to how your Python code produces its log likelihood. The two AIC scores you present agree to the second decimal.
